name: Iron Farm
produces: Iron ingots (3-5 per golem) and poppies
quickAnswer: An iron farm spawns iron golems on purpose, kills them with lava and collects the iron with hoppers. The designs are completely different per edition: Java uses 3 villagers scared by a zombie; Bedrock needs 10 villagers, 20 beds and a big spawning floor.
mechanics: Java Edition: a villager that has slept and worked recently can spawn an iron golem when it does not detect one nearby. Scared villagers (who can see a zombie) spawn golems much faster. Golems spawn in a 16x12x16 box around the village center.

Bedrock Edition: iron golems spawn when a village has at least 10 villagers linked to 20 beds, and 75% of villagers have worked at their workstation that day. Golems spawn in a 16x6x16 area around the village center.
In both editions the kill system is the same: water pushes the golem into lava blades that kill it without destroying the drops, and hoppers feed chests.
materials: 3 villagers + 3 beds + 3 workstations (Java) or 10 villagers + 20 beds (Bedrock)
1 zombie in a name-tagged boat or minecart (Java only)
~200 building blocks for the pods and platform
Water buckets, 4-8 hoppers, 1-2 chests, lava bucket, signs or trapdoors to hold the lava
steps: Java: build a spawning platform (at least 8x8) 6+ blocks above the villagers, with water channels flowing to a central lava kill hole.
Java: place 3 villagers in pods below with their beds and workstations, and position the zombie so all three can see it but it cannot reach them. Nametag the zombie so it never despawns.
Bedrock: build a 20x20-ish floor with 20 beds, bring 10 villagers with workstations, and make the spawning floor where golems appear a separate platform with the same lava-and-hopper kill setup.
Both: golems spawn on the platform, water pushes them into lava, iron falls into hoppers. Check that no caves or ground near the platform can steal spawns.
Both: build at least 8 blocks above ground and 80+ blocks from any real village so the centers do not merge.
rates: A simple Java 3-villager design produces roughly 300-400 iron ingots per hour. Bigger multi-module designs pass 1,000/hour. Bedrock rates are lower for the same footprint.
tips: Keep every spawnable block outside the platform slabs or leaf-covered so golems can only spawn in the water.
The zombie must see the villagers through a gap - trapdoors work well as a sightline.
If rates drop to zero in Java, a golem is probably stuck somewhere: villagers stop spawning while one is detected nearby.
keywords: iron farm minecraft java bedrock villagers zombie golem iron per hour

name: Mob Farm (XP and Drops)
produces: Gunpowder, bones, string, arrows, rotten flesh - and XP if you kill by hand
quickAnswer: A mob farm is a dark box where hostile mobs spawn, get flushed by water into a drop chute and land at your feet with half a heart - one punch each, and the XP and drops are yours. Build it high over an ocean so caves cannot steal the spawns.
mechanics: Hostile mobs spawn at light level 0 on solid blocks, in a sphere around the player: 24 to 128 blocks away in Java.
Rates depend entirely on how many other dark spots exist nearby - spawnproofing caves below or building 100+ blocks above the ocean surface is what makes a farm fast.
Fall damage math: mobs take 1 damage per block after the first 3, so a 22-block drop leaves zombies and skeletons (20 HP) at half a heart. Give spiders a different chute or they climb.
Bedrock rates are much lower than Java for the same design, and simulation distance limits the spawning area.
materials: ~500-1500 solid blocks for platforms and the chute (cobblestone is fine)
Slabs, trapdoors and water buckets for the flush system
4-8 hoppers and chests for collection
Torches to light the outside when you are done
steps: Pick an ocean biome and pillar up: build the collection point at least 100 blocks above the water so the farm is the only spawnable space in range.
Build 2-4 spawning platforms (about 8x8 each) with 2-block ceilings so endermen cannot spawn, water on the edges pushing to the center hole.
Drop chute: 22 blocks for one-punch kills, or 24+ for automatic kills if you only want drops (no XP).
Stand at the bottom with a Looting III sword: one hit kills each mob and multiplies the drops.
Light the roof and every outside surface when finished so mobs only spawn inside.
rates: A basic single-player tower gives a few thousand items per hour in Java with good positioning. Bedrock designs produce less - expect a fraction of Java rates.
tips: AFK spot matters: in Java, stand so the platforms are 24-40 blocks from you - closer than 24 blocks and nothing spawns.
Add a roof of slabs: phantoms spawn above you if you AFK outdoors for days.
Creepers only: build with trapdoors on the ceiling - creepers are shorter than zombies and skeletons.
keywords: mob farm xp farm minecraft gunpowder bones creeper farm dark room spawner

name: Automatic Sugarcane Farm
produces: Sugar cane (paper for books, rockets and trading)
quickAnswer: Plant sugar cane on a waterline, place a piston facing it at height 3 and an observer watching the top: when the cane grows to 3 blocks, the observer fires the piston and the cane drops into water streams leading to hoppers. Fully automatic, works in both editions.
mechanics: Sugar cane grows only on dirt, sand, grass, podzol or similar blocks directly next to water, up to 3 blocks tall.
Growth is random-tick based and identical in Java and Bedrock - the same design works in both.
An observer facing the cane detects the growth to height 3 and pulses the piston below it, breaking the top two blocks while the base stays planted.
Broken cane falls into flowing water channels that feed hoppers and chests.
materials: Per module: 1 observer, 1 piston, 1-3 building blocks, 1 sugar cane, water source
Hoppers + chest for collection (1 hopper per 2-4 modules is enough)
Solid blocks to wall the farm so cane cannot fly out
steps: Dig a trench for the waterline and plant sugar cane along both sides.
At height 2 behind the cane, place a row of pistons facing the cane; at height 3 place observers facing the cane, touching each piston's back.
Wire the observers to the pistons (the observer faces the cane, its output touches the piston - no redstone dust needed).
Add a water stream or hopper line under the cane to collect the drops into a chest.
Scale by repeating modules side by side and stacking floors on top.
rates: Each plant grows to harvest height every few minutes on average; a 20-cane module produces roughly a stack per hour. Stack floors for real volume.
tips: Bone meal does not work on sugar cane in Java (it does in Bedrock) - wait for natural growth in Java.
Feed the cane to a fletcher-adjacent setup: paper to librarians, rockets for elytra, sugar for cake.
Cover the water with lily pads or buttons if items get stuck.
keywords: sugar cane farm automatic observer piston minecraft paper rockets

name: Gold and XP Farm
produces: Gold nuggets, gold ingots, rotten flesh - and huge amounts of XP
quickAnswer: In Java, zombified piglins spawn inside large nether portal frames - build giant portals, funnel the piglins into a kill zone and swing your sword for endless gold and XP. In Bedrock, portals do not spawn piglins; use a zombified piglin platform farm in the nether wastes with a trident killer instead.
mechanics: Java: every active nether portal block can spawn a zombified piglin at light level 11 or lower - bigger portals and more frames mean more spawns. Many designs stack portals above the Nether bedrock ceiling (build limit) for maximum rates.
Bedrock: zombified piglins spawn naturally throughout the nether wastes; farms use big spawn platforms at low Y with turtle-egg bait or drop chutes, and a trident killer for AFK XP.
Trident killer (Bedrock + works in Java): pistons push a thrown trident back and forth, killing mobs while crediting you with the kill - full XP while AFK.
materials: Java: obsidian for the biggest portal frames you can build (a max portal is 23x23 inside) plus flint and steel
Collection: turtle egg (bait), magma blocks or fall damage, hoppers and chests
Looting III sword for manual killing; a trident with Loyalty for a trident killer
Bedrock variant: ~1000 blocks for spawn platforms and the trident killer (pistons, observers, lever)
steps: Java: build one or more max-size portals in the Nether, ideally on the nether roof (above Y=128) where no other spawns compete.
Lure or flush piglins to a kill chamber: they path toward turtle eggs and fall into the collection point.
Kill with a Looting III sword sweep for gold nuggets (craft into ingots) plus XP, or set a trident killer for AFK mode.
Bedrock: build large platforms in a nether wastes area around Y=30-40, drop the piglins 22+ blocks to a trident killer, and AFK nearby.
Store the rotten flesh for cleric trading - 32 flesh per emerald turns the byproduct into emeralds.
rates: Portal-based Java farms are among the fastest XP sources in the game - level 30 in a couple of minutes of swinging, plus chests of gold per hour. Bedrock platform farms are slower but still top-tier XP.
tips: Keep anger management in mind: hitting one piglin angers the group, which is exactly what you want at the kill point and nowhere else.
Gold feeds bartering farms (piglin bartering for pearls, quartz, obsidian) and golden apples/carrots.
On Java, building on the nether roof requires breaking bedrock or ender-pearling up - check current methods for your version.
keywords: gold farm xp farm zombified piglin portal farm trident killer minecraft

name: Raid Farm
produces: Totems of undying, emeralds, enchanted books, redstone, glowstone, saddles
quickAnswer: A raid farm triggers Bad Omen raids at a pillager outpost on purpose, funnels every wave into a kill zone and harvests the drops: totems from evokers, emeralds from everyone, and witch loot on top. It is the most loot-dense farm in the game - and one of the most complex to build.
mechanics: Kill a pillager captain (banner carrier) to get Bad Omen - since 1.21 captains drop an Ominous Bottle you drink when ready, which makes timing the farm far easier.
Entering a village with Bad Omen starts a raid: waves of pillagers, vindicators, evokers, witches and ravagers scale with difficulty and Bad Omen level.
Farm designs define an artificial 'village' (beds + workstations) near the outpost so raids trigger where you want, then push raid mobs into lava blades, fall damage or a trident killer.
Raid mobs drop emeralds and enchanted books (vindicators/pillagers), totems (evokers, always 1), redstone/glowstone/gunpowder (witches) and saddles (ravagers).
materials: A pillager outpost with spawn-proofed surroundings
Villager pods (2-3 villagers with beds and workstations) to anchor the raid location
Water streams, lava, signs, ~1000 building blocks, hoppers and storage for the output
Trident killer for AFK XP mode (optional)
steps: Find a pillager outpost and flatten or slab everything around it except the spots you want captains to spawn on.

Build the artificial village pods at the correct distance so the raid triggers at the outpost but the mobs spawn in your funnel - this distance is edition-specific, so follow a design made for your exact version.
Drink an Ominous Bottle at the outpost, walk to the village marker to start the raid, and let the water channels deliver each wave to the kill zone.
Kill evokers before they summon vexes - totems are the prize. Looting III multiplies the emeralds.
Repeat: raid farms chain raids continuously once the timing is set up.
rates: Top Java designs produce thousands of emeralds per hour plus stacks of totems. Even simple outpost farms out-earn almost any other loot source.
tips: Bad Omen level sets the wave count: level 5 Ominous Bottles (from higher-level captains) give the longest raids.
Keep the villagers unreachable: one ravager in the pod ends the farm until you restock.
Designs break between versions more than any other farm - verify the design matches your game version exactly, and note that Java and Bedrock raid spawning works completely differently.
keywords: raid farm totem farm bad omen ominous bottle pillager outpost emerald farm

name: Witch Farm
produces: Gunpowder, glowstone dust, redstone, glass bottles, sticks, sugar and spider eyes (4-8 items per witch)
quickAnswer: A witch hut is the only place witches spawn on demand: in Java, witches spawn inside the hut's bounding box at low light, so you floor the whole box, funnel witches to a kill spot and loot their potion ingredients. Bedrock hut rates are much lower - raid farms beat them there.
mechanics: Java Edition: witches spawn anywhere inside the hut's bounding box (a 7x7x4-ish volume) when the light level is 0. Removing the hut's blocks does not remove the spawn zone - the bounding box is what matters.
Java: witches count toward the hostile mob cap, so lighting every cave and surface within 128 blocks of the farm massively boosts rates.
Bedrock Edition: witches spawn only on the hut floor itself at low rates. Most Bedrock players get witch drops from raid farms instead.
Witches drink healing, fire resistance and water breathing potions mid-fight - kill them fast or by suffocation/fall damage so drops are guaranteed.
materials: Slabs and solid blocks to cover the bounding box with spawning floors
Water buckets for collection streams
Hoppers and chests
Torches or glow lichen to light the surroundings
Building blocks for the AFK platform
steps: Find a witch hut in a swamp biome (/locate structure minecraft:swamp_hut).
Java: demolish the hut and build 2-3 spawning floors inside the bounding box, with water channels pushing witches off the edge into a drop or killing chamber.
Java: light every cave and surface within 128 blocks - this step decides your rates.
Build an AFK spot ~120 blocks above the swamp so only the farm's floors are in spawning range.
Collect at the chests: gunpowder for rockets, glowstone and redstone for brewing, bottles for honey and potion work.
rates: A good Java perimeter-lit witch farm produces 1,000+ witch drops per hour. Unlit single-hut farms give a trickle. Bedrock huts are barely worth farming - use raids.
tips: The bounding box survives demolishing the hut: use a tool like Chunkbase with your seed to see it exactly.
Triple-hut seeds (three huts in range of one AFK spot) triple the output - hunt one if you are starting a long-term world.
Cats from the hut keep spawning as pets - free creeper repellent.
keywords: witch farm hut swamp gunpowder glowstone redstone potion drops

name: Automatic Pumpkin and Melon Farm
quickAnswer: Pumpkin and melon stems grow a fruit on a random adjacent dirt block. An observer watching that spot fires a piston the moment the fruit appears, breaking it into a hopper. Repeat the module in rows for infinite pumpkins and melons.
mechanics: A planted stem matures, then grows a pumpkin or melon on a random adjacent farmland/dirt/grass block with air above - the same stem fruits again and again.
An observer facing the fruit spot detects the fruit appearing and outputs a one-tick pulse: perfect for firing a piston.
The piston breaks the fruit (melons drop 3-7 slices), and a hopper minecart or hopper line collects it.
Bone meal speeds up stem growth but not fruiting - the fruiting itself is random-tick based.
materials: Pumpkin or melon seeds (chest loot, or craft from found fruit)
Farmland, water to hydrate it, and light (torches or glowstone)
1 observer + 1 piston per fruit spot
Hoppers or a hopper minecart rail below, plus chests
Building blocks for rows
steps: Till a hydrated farmland row and plant stems with one empty dirt block beside each stem (the fruit spot).
Place an observer facing each fruit spot (its face toward the spot, red dot toward the piston).
Put a piston beside each spot so it pushes across and breaks the fruit the instant it grows.
Run hoppers or a hopper minecart track under the row into chests.
Light the whole build 24/7 so stems keep working, and stack floors vertically for volume.
rates: A single module fruits every few minutes; a 20-module double row produces several stacks per hour of each crop with zero player input.
tips: Melon slices are the backbone of glistening melons for healing potions; pumpkins trade to farmer villagers for emeralds (6 pumpkins = 1 emerald at apprentice level).
Keep the fruit spot as the ONLY valid growth spot per stem by slab-proofing other adjacent blocks - the observer then never misses.
Jack o'lanterns from pumpkin + torch make great underwater lighting.
keywords: pumpkin farm melon automatic observer piston villager trading

name: Bamboo Farm
produces: Bamboo for fuel, sticks, scaffolding and pandas
quickAnswer: Bamboo grows up to 16 blocks tall and fast. An observer at height detects the shoot reaching it and fires pistons that break the whole column above the base - fully automatic bamboo with one module per plant.
mechanics: Bamboo grows one block at random ticks, up to 12-16 blocks tall, and each plant grows independently and much faster than other crops.
Breaking any part of the column drops everything above it - so one piston break near the base harvests the entire plant.
An observer watching a set height fires when the bamboo reaches it; pistons or a flying machine do the rest.
Java flying-machine harvesters clear huge fields; single-column observer modules work identically in both editions.
materials: Bamboo (jungle biomes, jungle temple chests, fishing in jungles, shipwreck supply chests)
Observer + piston per column
Hoppers and chests
Light sources
Optional (Java): slime blocks, honey blocks and observers for a flying machine
steps: Plant bamboo rows on dirt, grass or sand with space above.
Place a piston at the second block height of each plant, facing the bamboo.
Put an observer above the piston, facing the bamboo, wired so its pulse fires the piston when the shoot grows into its face.
Run a water stream or hopper line below to carry drops to chests.
For big volume in Java, build a flying machine that sweeps a whole field and returns on a timer.
rates: A single-column module gives roughly one bamboo every few minutes; a 20-plant wall produces several stacks per hour - enough to run furnaces forever.
tips: Bamboo smelts 0.25 items each (4 bamboo per item) - crafting it into bamboo blocks first smelts 1.5 items per block, a more efficient fuel.
Feed pandas bamboo to breed them; hearts show when they are happy.
Scaffolding (6 bamboo + 1 string) is the best building-access block in the game - the farm pays for itself fast.

name: Guardian XP Farm
produces: Prismarine shards, prismarine crystals, fish and massive XP
quickAnswer: Guardians spawn in water inside the ocean monument's bounding box. Drain or section the monument, funnel guardians into a kill tube, and one-hit them with a Looting III sword for the best combined XP and prismarine farm in the game.

Bedrock designs typically section spawn spots with water columns since draining is harder; rates are lower but still strong.
A 23-block drop leaves guardians at one hit; Looting III multiplies shards and crystals.
materials: Hundreds of sand or gravel for dividing walls (draining approach)
Sponges from the monument's sponge rooms
Building blocks, signs, soul sand for bubble columns
Hoppers, chests, and a Looting III sword
Conduit or water breathing potions for construction
steps: Kill the three elder guardians first to stop Mining Fatigue.
Wall off the monument exterior with sand/gravel and sponge-drain the interior (Java), or section spawn areas in Bedrock.
Build the collection system: water or bubble columns pushing guardians to a central 1x1 drop chute.
Stand at the kill spot with Looting III: one sword swing per guardian, XP orbs stream in.
Route drops to chests and smelt the fish overflow if you want cooked food too.
rates: Drained Java monument farms are among the fastest XP sources in the game - level 30 in minutes - plus double-chests of prismarine per hour. Bedrock sectioned farms give solid XP and shards at a slower pace.
tips: The sponges you need to drain the monument are inside it - dry them in the Nether for instant reuse.
Guardian lasers hurt: build the kill spot so their line of sight breaks before you arrive.
Pair with a furnace array: raw cod overflow becomes a solid food supply.

name: Creeper Farm
produces: Gunpowder (0-2 per creeper, +1 with Looting) and music discs if you route skeletons to the kill
quickAnswer: A creeper farm is a mob farm tuned so only creepers can spawn: trapdoors on the ceiling make the spawning space 1.7 blocks tall (too short for zombies and skeletons), and carpets break up spider spawns. Cats scare the creepers into the drop chute.
mechanics: Creepers are 1.7 blocks tall - placing trapdoors on the ceiling of each spawning layer leaves a space zombies and skeletons (both around 2 blocks) cannot spawn in, while creepers still can.
Spiders would still fit, so scatter carpets or buttons on the floor to break up the 3x3 area spiders need to spawn.
Creepers flee from cats within a 6-block radius - a cat sitting in the middle of each layer scares creepers off the platform and into the collection chute far faster than waiting for them to wander.
Like any mob farm, build it high above the ocean or light up every cave in a 128-block radius so the mob cap fills only inside your farm.
Bonus: if you ever want music discs, a creeper killed by a skeleton's arrow drops one of 12 discs - a separate trapped-skeleton setup handles that.
materials: ~1,000 building blocks (slabs and trapdoors multiply fast)
A stack or more of trapdoors per layer (any wood)
1-3 tamed cats in minecart-proof spots
Carpets or buttons (spider-proofing)
Hoppers, chests and a kill or drop system
steps: Pick a spot: high over a deep ocean is the lazy option - no caves to light. Otherwise slab or torch every cave within 128 blocks.
Build the spawning tower: dark layers of at least 10x10, each 2 blocks of air high, with open trapdoors lining the ceiling so the effective height is 1.7 blocks.
Spider-proof the floors: a checkerboard of carpets every third block leaves creepers room but denies spiders their 3x3 spawn area.
Seat the cats: one cat per layer in a safe alcove at the center - creepers within 6 blocks panic and run straight off the edges.
Add the drop: water streams or open edges funnel creepers into a central chute - a 22-block drop leaves them one hit from death, or let the fall finish them.
Collect with hoppers into chests; wear Looting III if you kill by hand for up to 3 gunpowder per creeper.
AFK at the right spot: 24+ blocks from the nearest spawning space and under 128 from the furthest, so mobs spawn but do not despawn.
Scale it: more layers and a perimeter (spawn-proofing the ground below) multiply rates fast.
rates: A simple two-layer design gives a few hundred gunpowder per hour; optimized multi-layer Java farms with cat scare and a full perimeter reach several thousand per hour. Bedrock rates run lower because natural spawning is slower.
tips: Use any wood trapdoors - they are only there to shave height off the spawning space.
Build over deep ocean first; lighting 128 blocks of caves is the slowest part of any mob farm.
Keep the cats safe: a loose cat wanders off, and a dead cat turns your farm into a waiting room.
Pair it with a sugarcane farm and you have infinite rockets for your elytra.
keywords: creeper farm minecraft, gunpowder farm minecraft, how to farm gunpowder minecraft, creeper farm tutorial, music disc farm minecraft

name: Enderman Farm
produces: Ender pearls and huge amounts of XP (5 XP per enderman)
quickAnswer: An enderman farm sits in the End: a spawning platform 128+ blocks from the main island, an endermite bait in a minecart that endermen hate on sight, and a 43-block drop that leaves them at one hit. The fastest XP farm in the game.
mechanics: Endermen spawn constantly across the End's islands - but the farm works by building the only spawning spaces within 128 blocks of the AFK spot, far out in the void.
The bait: an endermite has a 5% chance to spawn when a thrown ender pearl lands. Name it with a name tag immediately - an unnamed endermite despawns within 2 minutes, even in a minecart.
Endermen within 64 blocks with line of sight charge the endermite to kill it - that hatred walks them straight off the platform and down the chute.
A drop of 43 blocks leaves endermen at half a heart - one punch kills, and XP flows at full speed.
In Bedrock the endermite spawns where the pearl lands (in Java it spawns at your original position), and Bedrock endermites fight back - the bait-in-minecart design works in both.
materials: Access to the End (beat the dragon first)
~2 ender pearls to spawn the endermite + 1 name tag + 1 minecart
Several stacks of leaf blocks or slabs for the platform and the 128-block bridge
Hoppers and chests for the pearls, an ender chest for overflow
steps: Beat the ender dragon, then bridge or pearl 128+ blocks away from the main island in any direction - the void is your spawn-proofing.
Build the spawning platform: a big slab-free pad (20x20 or larger) with a 2x2 hole in the middle, 3 blocks of headroom.
Set the bait: throw pearls until an endermite appears (5% chance each), catch it in a minecart over the hole, and name it before 2 minutes pass.
Build the drop chute below the hole: 43 blocks of fall leaves endermen one hit from death; 44+ kills them outright if you only want pearls.
Add the kill floor: a safe spot at the bottom where you swipe at their feet - sweeping-edge swords hit whole groups in Java.
Stand on the AFK spot: endermen spawn on the platform, aggro the endermite from 64 blocks away, path to it and fall.
Collect: hoppers under the kill floor feed chests; expect to fill them with pearls faster than you can use them.
Repair your gear for free: the XP stream mends every mending item you hold or wear in seconds.
rates: A well-built enderman farm is one of the fastest XP sources in the game - around level 30 in a minute at full speed - and produces ender pearls by the chest. Even a rough first build reaches level 30 in a few minutes.
tips: Name the endermite the moment it lands - forgetting the name tag is the number one way these farms die.
Build the platform from bottom slabs or leaves while you work so nothing spawns on your construction site.
Bring a pumpkin helmet for the walk back: one accidental glance at the main island's endermen ends trips early.
Void-side rails beat bridges: a minecart line from the outer End islands makes restocking painless.
keywords: enderman farm minecraft, xp farm minecraft end, ender pearl farm minecraft, endermite farm tutorial, fastest xp farm minecraft

name: Wither Skeleton Farm
produces: Wither skeleton skulls (2.5% per kill, up to 5.5% with Looting III in Java / 8.5% in Bedrock), bones and coal
quickAnswer: Wither skeletons spawn only in nether fortresses. A farm strips the fortress down to spawning platforms, carpets it with wither roses - where only wither skeletons can spawn - and funnels them to a kill zone for skulls, the key to summoning the wither.
mechanics: Wither skeletons spawn in nether fortresses at light level 0-7: on nether bricks anywhere in the fortress's outer bounding box, and on any block inside each structure piece's own box.
They are the only mobs that can spawn on wither roses (immune to the wither effect) - covering every spawning block in roses makes the farm spawn wither skeletons exclusively.
They are 2.4 blocks tall, so they need 3 blocks of clearance - 2-block ceilings elsewhere suppress them, which is how designs concentrate spawns.
Skulls only drop from player kills: 2.5% base, +1% per Looting level in Java (5.5% at Looting III) and +2% in Bedrock (8.5% at Looting III). Charged creeper explosions also drop skulls.
Spawn-proofing matters as much as the farm: every other fortress mob (blazes, zombified piglins, magma cubes) competes for the mob cap, so slab or rose everything nearby.
materials: A nether fortress - ideally where several structure pieces overlap (intersections multiply spawn spaces)
Hundreds of wither roses (farm them with a simple wither cage setup, or use slab spawn-proofing instead)
Building blocks, slabs and glass for platforms and spawn-proofing
A sword with Looting III, and ideally Smite (wither skeletons are undead)
steps: Scout a fortress: the best spots are intersections where two or more structure bounding boxes overlap - more bounding box means more spawn attempts.
Clear the space: strip towers, blaze spawners and decoration down to flat nether brick platforms inside the bounding boxes.
Spawn-proof everything else: slab, button or glass every block within 128 blocks that is not part of your farm - netherrack plains, other fortress corridors, all of it.
Choose the rose method or the height method: wither roses on the platforms allow only wither skeletons, while 2-block ceilings everywhere except your platforms do the same job for free.
Build the funnel: open edges or water-free push systems (no water in the Nether - use trapdoors, turtle eggs or open drops) herd skeletons to one kill point.
Kill by hand with Looting III: every skull run averages one skull per 18 kills in Java, one per 12 in Bedrock.
Bring smite: one Smite V hit kills a wither skeleton through armor, and fire resistance makes the blazes you missed irrelevant.
Scale up: clear more bounding box, add platforms, and rates climb - three skulls means a wither on demand, and beacons follow.
rates: A basic single-intersection farm with Looting III gives a skull every few minutes of active killing; fully cleared Java designs with wither roses produce skulls fast enough to make beacons a renewable resource. Coal and bones pile up for free.
tips: Check the seed map: fortresses generate in bands along the Z axis - if one is far, another sits at the same Z to the east or west.
The wither effect from their hits ignores armor and drains your health bar black - milk does not cure Wither, so do not get surrounded.
Kill some blazes while you are there: you will want the rods for brewing stands and eyes of ender anyway.
A charged creeper kill guarantees the skull - some players trap one as a skull insurance policy.
keywords: wither skeleton farm minecraft, wither skull farm minecraft, nether fortress farm, how to get wither skeleton skulls, wither rose farm minecraft

name: Blaze Farm
produces: Blaze rods (0-1 per blaze, +1 with Looting, player kills only) and 10 XP per blaze
quickAnswer: A blaze farm cages one of the blaze spawners found in nether fortress towers, funnels the blazes into a kill chamber and farms rods and XP. Blazes spawn at light level 11 or less, so light-level-15 blocks like glowstone switch the spawner off while you build.
mechanics: Blazes spawn naturally only in nether fortresses, at light level 11 or less - and every fortress generates up to two blaze spawner platforms on fenced towers reached by a three-block staircase.
Rods drop only from player (or tamed wolf) kills: 0-1 blaze rods, +0-1 with Looting. Blazes also drop 10 XP - double a normal mob - which is why blaze farms double as solid XP farms.
Because blazes need light level 11 or less, you can pause a spawner completely by surrounding it with light-level-15 blocks (glowstone, lanterns, shroomlights) and re-open it by removing them.
Blazes shoot volleys of three small fireballs and set you on fire - fire resistance makes the whole farm safe, and snowballs deal 3 damage to blazes if you want a cheap ranged option.
Unlike most farms, the spawner does the work: you do not need spawn-proofing beyond the spawner's own range, just a funnel and a kill spot.
materials: A nether fortress with a blaze spawner
Glowstone or other light-15 blocks to disable the spawner while building
Building blocks and slabs for the funnel and kill chamber
Fire resistance potions, a good sword (Smite does nothing - blazes are not undead), optional Looting III
Hoppers and chests for the rods
steps: Find the spawner: blaze towers stick out of fortress walkways - a fenced platform with a cage spawner and a three-block stair. Bring blocks; the walk there is the dangerous part.
Disable it first: place glowstone (or any light-15 block) on and around the spawner so no blazes spawn while you build. Drink fire resistance anyway.
Build the funnel: enclose the spawner area and shape a chute so blazes, which float upward, get pushed by open trapdoors, signs or your own knockback toward one collection point.
Add the kill chamber: a spot where blaze feet are exposed but their fireballs cannot reach you - half-slabs or a lava-free grinder. Blazes take damage from water, so no water streams in the Nether.
Re-enable the spawner by removing the glowstone, and stand close: spawners run only when a player is within 16 blocks.
Kill with Looting III: each blaze averages about one rod per two kills, and the 10 XP each adds up to levels fast.
AFK is not an option here - rods require player kills - but a few minutes of swinging per session covers all brewing needs.
Mark the way home: nether fortresses all look alike, so leave a torch trail or coordinates.
rates: A single caged spawner with Looting III gives roughly a stack of blaze rods per 20 minutes of active killing, plus enough XP for several enchantments. Two-spawner fortresses double that if both towers are close.
tips: Light-15 blocks are your off switch - glowstone on every face of the spawner cage stops spawns completely while you work.
Fire resistance turns the scariest part of the farm into background noise; never farm blazes without it.
Snowballs hurt blazes (3 damage each) - a dispenser or a stack in hand finishes low-health blazes safely.
Grab a second spawner only if it sits within about 16 blocks of the first - otherwise one caged spawner already outpaces your rod use.

name: Slime Farm
produces: Slimeballs (0-2 per small slime, +1 with Looting) - a large slime yields around 9 slimeballs on average
quickAnswer: Slimes spawn below Y=40 in special slime chunks (about 1 in 10 chunks, any light level) or on swamp surfaces between Y=51-69, most on full moons. Dig out a slime chunk, bait the slimes with an iron golem and let gravity or magma do the killing.
mechanics: About 1 in 10 Overworld chunks is a slime chunk: slimes spawn there below Y=40 in any light and any weather. In Java the chunks depend on your world seed; in Bedrock they are the same coordinates in every world.

The swamp option: slimes also spawn in swamps and mangrove swamps between Y=51-69 at light level 7 or less - most often on a full moon and never on a new moon. No digging required, but rates follow the moon cycle.
Slimes seek a player or, failing that, an iron golem within 16 blocks - a caged iron golem pulls every slime in the farm toward the kill zone automatically.

Big and medium slimes split into smaller ones on death; only the smallest size drops slimeballs (0-2, +1 with Looting). Frogs eat small slimes outright and drop slimeballs - a frog-powered kill chamber skips the splitting.
Because slime chunks ignore light, you light the farm for safety without hurting rates - unlike every other mob farm.
materials: A slime chunk (chunk finders online use your seed; in Bedrock, any published slime-chunk map works for every world)
Pickaxes and patience: the classic design digs the whole chunk out below Y=40
1 iron golem + blocks to cage it, or a few frogs
Torches, hoppers, chests, and magma blocks or campfires for the kill floor
Optional: water to push slimes (they float and flail, but currents still move them)
steps: Find your chunk: plug your seed into a slime chunk finder (Java) or look up the universal Bedrock chunk map - then mark the 16x16 area on the surface.
Dig it out: excavate the chunk from Y=39 down in layers, leaving 3-block-high platforms every few layers - more floor space means more spawns.
Light everything: torches everywhere. Slimes do not care about light, but creepers do spawn in the dark and they wreck farms.
Set the bait: cage an iron golem on a pillar in the center, or park frogs along the kill floor - slimes path toward golems within 16 blocks, frogs simply eat the small ones.
Add the kill floor: magma blocks, campfires or a long drop under each platform finishes what the fall and the frogs start.
Collect below: hoppers under the kill floor feed chests of slimeballs.
AFK 24-128 blocks away: close enough to keep the chunk loaded and spawning, far enough that slimes keep moving.
Scale by digging more chunks or adding layers - a fully dug multi-layer slime chunk is a sticky piston supply for life.
rates: A single dug-out slime chunk with several platforms and golem bait produces hundreds of slimeballs per hour; a swamp full-moon night is slower but needs zero digging. One large slime averages about 9 slimeballs after all splits.
tips: In Bedrock you can check any slime chunk map without knowing your seed - the chunks are identical in every world.
Keep the platforms 3 blocks high so big slimes fit and split all the way down.
Frogs are the elegant kill method: they one-shot small slimes and still drop the slimeballs.
Bring a Looting III sword for AFK-free sessions - every small slime you finish by hand drops up to 3 slimeballs.
keywords: slime farm minecraft, slime chunk minecraft, slimeball farm tutorial, how to find slime chunks minecraft, swamp slime farm

name: Tree Farm
produces: Logs of every wood type, saplings, apples (oak and dark oak) and sticks from leftover leaves
quickAnswer: A tree farm is a planted grid of saplings you bone meal and chop on a loop. Dark oak grows only from 2x2 sapling squares, oaks and dark oaks drop apples, and a Fortune axe on the leaves pays the saplings back with interest.
mechanics: Saplings grow in two hidden stages: bone meal skips ahead instantly, while natural growth needs light level 9 or higher above the sapling - torches or glowstone keep a farm running underground or at night.
Dark oak, and the giant spruce, jungle and pale oak variants, grow only from four saplings planted in a 2x2 square - with nothing beside the north-western sapling up to the tree's full height.
Sapling economics: leaves drop saplings 1 in 20 (1 in 40 for jungle), so every tree more than replants itself. Fortune III on an axe roughly triples sapling and apple drops from leaves.
Oaks and dark oaks drop apples from their leaves - dark oak 2x2 farms are the classic renewable apple source.

Spruce 2x2 mega trees convert podzol and give the most wood per bonemeal, but their height (up to 31 blocks) makes manual harvesting slow - pick tree size to match how lazy you want the chopping to be.
materials: Saplings of your chosen wood (dark oak needs 4 per tree)
Bone meal - a composter loop or skeleton farm keeps you stocked
An axe, ideally Efficiency IV-V; Fortune III for leaf-clearing
Torches or glowstone for light level 9+ above every sapling
Optional: hoppers and chests for a collection pad
steps: Pick your tree: birch for easy chopping (max 7 tall), spruce or jungle 2x2 for bulk wood, dark oak 2x2 for apples and thick trunks.
Lay out the grid: single saplings every 4-5 blocks so canopies do not tangle; 2x2 squares spaced 6+ blocks apart for the giants.
Light it: torch every few blocks so the block above each sapling reads light level 9+ - underground farms need this, surface farms only at night.
Bone meal each sapling until the tree pops - one to three meals usually does it.
Chop from the top down or pillar up: birch and oak come down from the ground, mega trees want a spiral staircase of their own logs.
Replant immediately from your sapling stock - the farm only works as a loop.
Sweep the leaves with a Fortune axe for saplings, apples and sticks, or let them decay while you plant the next row.
Upgrade later: TNT-based blast chambers and wither-powered designs automate endgame wood, but a manual grid covers every survival need first.
rates: A 20-tree manual grid with bone meal yields several stacks of logs per ten-minute cycle and always pays its saplings back; dark oak 2x2 loops additionally return a steady trickle of apples.
tips: Birch is the beginner pick: it never grows tall variants, so every tree chops from flat ground.
For 2x2 trees, bone meal any of the four saplings - but keep the area around the north-west one clear or growth fails silently.
Compost your excess saplings: each has a 30% chance to raise the compost level, feeding bone meal back into the loop.
An Efficiency V diamond axe plus Haste from a beacon insta-mines logs - the single biggest quality-of-life upgrade for wood farming.

name: Kelp Farm
produces: Kelp for smelting into dried kelp - food, and dried kelp blocks that smelt 20 items each
quickAnswer: Kelp grows underwater in any ocean except warm and frozen ones. Plant it in a column of water, let it grow and break the second block from the bottom - the whole stalk above drops as items. Bone meal speeds it up, and smelted kelp becomes fuel that smelts other kelp.
mechanics: Kelp only grows underwater, planted on a block with a full top face (not magma) in a water source or downward-flowing water - and it lives in every ocean biome except warm, frozen and deep frozen oceans.
Each kelp plant has a hidden age (0-24, check with F3 in Java): every new block of growth adds 1, and at age 25 it stops - so natural stalks top out between 2 and 26 blocks tall.

The farmer's trick: breaking any kelp block re-randomizes the age of the block below it, so stalks keep regrowing - and breaking the second block from the bottom drops the entire upper stalk as items at once.
Bone meal works on kelp - a dispenser with bone meal under each plant turns a slow natural farm into a fast one.

Fuel math: 9 dried kelp craft into a dried kelp block, which smelts 20 items (2.5x coal per item slot). Net gain is 11 smelts per block after the kelp you burned to dry it - use lava buckets or campfires for the first drying and the loop is pure profit.
Smelting kelp also gives XP - a kelp farm feeding furnaces doubles as a quiet, safe XP bank when you empty the furnaces by hand.
materials: A few kelp from any cold or lukewarm ocean
Building blocks for the water column (glass to watch it grow)
Water buckets
Dispensers + bone meal + observers for the automatic version
Furnaces or smokers, and hoppers with chests
steps: Gather starter kelp: dive any ocean that is not warm or frozen - kelp breaks instantly by hand and the whole stalk above the break drops.
Build the column: a vertical water tube over a solid base block, one kelp planted at the bottom per column.
Harvest smart: break the second block from the bottom - the plant stays rooted and everything above pops off as items.
Automate it: an observer watching the top growth fires a piston that breaks the stalk, and water currents carry items to a hopper.
Add bone meal: a dispenser under the plant, triggered on a clock, forces constant growth - kelp accepts bone meal, unlike sugar cane or cactus.
Dry the kelp: furnaces or smokers turn kelp into dried kelp - eat it in a pinch, but craft 9 into blocks for fuel.
Close the loop: dried kelp blocks smelt 20 items each, so the farm fuels its own drying with plenty left over for your other smelting.
Harvest furnace XP by hand: pull the dried kelp out manually and the stored smelting XP flows to you.
rates: A single manual column yields a few kelp per minute; an observer-piston module with bone meal produces stacks per hour and fuels itself. One dried kelp block smelts 20 items - net +11 after drying costs.
tips: Plant on any full-top-face block except magma - magma turns the water column into a bubble elevator that sucks the kelp down.
Campfires dry kelp for free - slow, but the first batches cost zero fuel while the loop spins up.
Keep the farm in a spawn chunk or near your base: kelp only grows in loaded chunks like every crop.
A kelp column in a water stream converts flowing water into sources - the classic cheap bubble-elevator trick, free with the farm.

name: Cactus Farm
produces: Cactus for green dye and smelting XP (1 XP per smelt in Java, the highest of any farmable block; 0.2 in Bedrock)
quickAnswer: Cactus grows on sand with zero light and zero water, and it breaks itself when a block sits next to it - so a fence post at the right height makes every new segment harvest itself. Fully automatic, no bone meal needed (bone meal does not even work on cactus).
mechanics: Cactus grows only on sand, red sand, suspicious sand or another cactus - no light, no water, no bone meal. It adds one block every 16 random ticks, about 18 minutes on average, up to 3 blocks tall naturally.
The self-harvest rule: a cactus breaks and drops as an item the moment any solid block occupies a space beside it - a fence, string or sign at the third level breaks every new growth instantly.
Watch the drops: a cactus block destroys any item entity that touches it, including cactus items - collection hoppers must sit where drops cannot brush a cactus.

Smelting cactus gives green dye and, in Java, 1 XP per operation - the highest smelting XP of any farmable block. Big furnace arrays fed by cactus farms are classic XP banks: smelt all day, empty one furnace by hand, and levels pour out.
Cactus flowers (10% chance at 1-2 blocks tall, 25% at 3+) stop the cactus growing until removed - a bonus crop, not a problem, in automated designs that break growth anyway.
materials: Sand or red sand, one per cactus
Cactus starters from any desert or badlands
Fences, string, signs or trapdoors for the break layer
Hoppers and chests placed clear of the cactus hitboxes
Furnace array + fuel for the XP bank (optional)
steps: Pick the layout: rows of sand with cactus planted one block apart diagonally (they cannot touch), in a grid as dense as your space allows.
Set the break layer: a fence or string line at the height where the third block would grow - every new segment breaks itself the tick it appears.
Protect the drops: leave a full air gap between the cactus and any water channel or hopper - items that touch a cactus are destroyed.
Collect below: hoppers under the sand rows (or water streams leading to one) feed chests.
Scale wide, not tall: more plants beat more height - each cactus tops out at 3 blocks and only grows on its own random ticks.
Feed the XP bank: pipe cactus into a furnace array with any fuel, let it run, then pull a stack out by hand to cash the stored XP.
Harvest flowers by hand if you want them - the farm's broken growth never gives the plant time to flower anyway.
Go AFK anywhere in range: cactus grows on random ticks in loaded chunks, no player proximity required.
rates: Each cactus averages one new block every ~18 minutes, so rates scale purely with plant count - a few dozen plants with a furnace array bank noticeable XP per day in Java, plus stacks of green dye.
tips: Never let collection water touch a cactus side - one sloppy stream eats your entire output.
Java players: the 1 XP per smelt is a long-standing quirk Mojang marked as intended - enjoy it.
Badlands count too: red sand works exactly like sand for planting.
A cactus by your storage wall doubles as a trash can - throw junk at it and the items are destroyed safely.

name: Chorus Fruit Farm
produces: Chorus fruit (0-1 per plant block) for food and purpur blocks, plus chorus flowers to replant
quickAnswer: Chorus plants grow from chorus flowers planted on end stone - in any dimension, at any light level. Harvest the fruit by chopping the trunk (everything above breaks), shoot the flowers down with arrows to replant, and re-plant to reset their age.
mechanics: Chorus flowers plant only on end stone, but grow in any dimension and any light - an Overworld chorus farm beside your base works exactly like an End one.
Each flower ages as it grows and stops at age 5 (turning purple); harvesting and replanting the flower resets the age, so the same flowers serve forever.
Breaking any chorus plant block breaks everything above it - one axe swing at the trunk brings the whole tree down, each plant block rolling 0-1 chorus fruit (Fortune does not improve it).

The flowers are the catch: they drop themselves only when broken directly, shot with a projectile or blown up - if you break the supporting plant under them, they pop into nothing. Arrows are the classic harvest tool.
Chorus fruit teleports you a few blocks when eaten (like an enderman) - handy panic food - and smelts into popped chorus fruit, the recipe for purpur blocks and end rods.
materials: End stone (one block per flower)
Chorus flowers from the outer End islands
An axe for the trunks and a bow with arrows for the flowers
Torches optional - light does not matter
Furnace if you want purpur production
steps: Harvest starters in the End: bridge to the outer islands after the dragon fight and shoot the white flowers off the treetops - arrows drop them as items; breaking the trunk first destroys them.
Plant at home: end stone rows with a flower on each, spaced 3-4 blocks apart so the branching canopies do not tangle.
Let them grow: flowers branch upward and outward through age 4, then finish at age 5 - taller, bushier plants mean more fruit per harvest.
Harvest the fruit: chop the lowest plant block with an axe - the entire plant collapses, dropping 0-1 fruit per block.
Harvest the flowers separately: shoot or break each flower directly before or after felling the plant, or they vanish.
Replant immediately: each flower goes back on end stone with its age reset, ready for the next cycle.
Wait for full size for best rates: young plants give a few fruit; mature age-5 trees give dozens.
Process the surplus: eat it for the teleport, or smelt it into popped chorus fruit and craft purpur blocks and end rods for building.
rates: A mature grid of 20-30 fully grown plants yields several stacks of chorus fruit per harvest cycle; plants regrow from replanted flowers in a few in-game days, and the flowers last forever.
tips: Always carry a bow in the End: flowers destroyed with their support block drop nothing, and every lost flower is a lost tree.
Purple flowers are done growing - harvest those plants first; white flowers are still working.
Plant in the Overworld to skip the End commute entirely - end stone is the only requirement.
Do not stand in a corner when you eat chorus fruit: the random teleport can wedge you into a wall.
